items.prompt:
Prompt:

Character sheet created by GPT Image 2.5:

IMPORTANT — IDENTITY LOCK: The uploaded reference image is the definitive identity reference. Reproduce the EXACT SAME PERSON throughout the entire character sheet. Do NOT redesign, beautify, reinterpret, or replace the character. Preserve with maximum accuracy: exact facial identity, facial structure and proportions, eyes, eye shape and iris color, eyebrows and natural brow shape, nose shape and proportions, lips, mouth shape and fullness, cheeks, jawline and chin, skin tone and natural skin texture, age appearance, hairline, exact hair color, length, texture and hairstyle, body proportions and physique, distinctive facial characteristics.

CHARACTER SHEET LAYOUT: Create one clean, professional reference-board image containing: large front portrait / face close-up, front view, 3/4 left view, 3/4 right view, left profile, right profile, back view, full-body front view, full-body 3/4 view, full-body side view, full-body back view, neutral expression, natural smile, soft smile, looking left, looking right, eye close-up, eyebrow close-up, nose close-up, lips close-up, hair close-up, accessories close-up, outfit / clothing reference, color palette / skin-tone reference.

CONSISTENCY: Every panel must show the SAME person. Keep facial identity, proportions, hairstyle, skin tone, body shape, and physical characteristics consistent across every angle, pose, and expression. For views not clearly visible in the reference, intelligently reconstruct the character while staying strictly faithful to the visible reference. Do not invent major distinguishing features.

PRESENTATION: Premium professional film-production character bible / modeling reference sheet. Clean editorial layout. Neutral studio background. Soft realistic studio lighting. Sharp facial details. Natural skin pores and texture. Individual hair strands. Realistic fabric and accessories. Accurate human anatomy. Consistent camera perspective. Clean thin borders between panels. Professional labels underneath each view. Minimal elegant typography. High-end fashion / model reference aesthetic.

PHOTOREALISM: Ultra-photorealistic. Real human appearance. Natural skin texture. Realistic eyes. Physically accurate hair. Natural shadows. Realistic proportions. No CGI appearance. No plastic skin. No doll-like face. No artificial beauty-face replacement.

NEGATIVE PROMPT: different person, different face, face morphing, identity drift, altered facial structure, different eyes, different nose, different lips, different jawline, different skin tone, different hairstyle, inconsistent body proportions, duplicate person, distorted anatomy, asymmetrical face, plastic skin, waxy skin, CGI, 3D render, cartoon, anime, illustration, over-beautification, excessive makeup, unrealistic eyes, blurry face, low detail, extra fingers, missing fingers, malformed hands, bad anatomy.

OUTPUT: One complete, highly detailed professional CHARACTER CONSISTENCY SHEET in a single image, suitable as a master reference for generating consistent images and videos of this character.

Video created by Seedance 2.5:

SCENE: A day in New York shot entirely by the subject herself: waking in her hotel suite, coffee, getting ready, out into the city, back to the room at night.

ACTIVE REFERENCES: @image1 — the hotel suite. Curved cove ceiling with warm LED coving, deep red carpet, cream walls, two black organic sculptures above a light wood headboard, white bedding with red pillows, twin bedside lamps, pale sofa, oval coffee table, sheer curtains, dark door. @image2 — the subject. Young woman, shoulder-length wavy blonde hair with curtain bangs and highlights, light freckles, thin gold necklace, silver ring, dark brown off-the-shoulder knit with white diamond-stripe pattern. 100% matches the reference.

CAMERA OWNERSHIP LOCK: Only two positions exist. HELD: arm extended, camera 0.4–0.7m from her face, visible arm tension, tilt and step-bounce. PROPPED: camera on a surface she placed it on, crooked and fixed, with her moving in and out of frame. No operator shots, no tracking, nothing she could not have filmed alone.

FORMAT: Eight shots, 30s, seven hard cuts, no fades. Real-time.

0–4s SHOT 1 — PROPPED, morning room. Camera on the sideboard 3m from the bed at 1.1m, static and tilted. The suite matches @image1: cove light on, curtains half open, cool daylight across the red carpet. @image2 is visible at 0.0s, sitting up on the bed edge. She rubs her face and says to the running camera: “It’s seven. In New York. Why am I awake.” She stands and walks out screen-right. HARD CUT.

4–7s SHOT 2 — HELD, window light. Arm’s length, above eye line. She pulls the curtain, squints at the street below, then looks into the lens: “Okay. It’s actually happening.” Arm wobble throughout. HARD CUT.

7–11s SHOT 3 — PROPPED, coffee. Camera on the oval coffee table, low, looking up past a cup. She sits into frame, pours, tastes, and says: “Hotel coffee. We’ll fix that outside.” Steam bends in the light. HARD CUT.

11–15s SHOT 4 — HELD, mirror. Camera at chest height reflected in the suite mirror. She works through her hair with the other hand. At 13s: “This is as good as it gets. Let’s go.” HARD CUT.

15–18s SHOT 5 — HELD, leaving. Camera held low at waist height, turned forward. She crosses the red carpet to the door. She opens it and corridor light floods the frame. Off-frame: “Downtown first.” HARD CUT.

18–22s SHOT 6 — PROPPED, street. Camera on a stoop rail, static and crooked. A New York block behind her: brownstone steps, fire escapes, yellow cabs, steam from a vent. She walks in from screen-left, stands in frame, and says: “Look at this street.” Then walks to the lens and takes it. Passers-by cross the foreground. HARD CUT.

22–26s SHOT 7 — PROPPED, diner. Camera on the counter behind a plate, looking up. She sits into frame, takes a bite, eyes widen, and says: “Okay, that’s the one.” She laughs and keeps eating. HARD CUT.

26–30s SHOT 8 — HELD, night, back in the room. She lies back across the white bedding, hair spread, in the brown knit again. Bedside lamps and cove light are the only sources. Into the lens: “Twenty thousand steps. Everything hurts.” Softer: “Same time tomorrow.” She waves as she lowers the camera. 30.0s black.

SPEECH: Only the quoted lines are spoken, at the timings given, all in her voice. Lips still at all other times. No voiceover, no second speaker, no offscreen voices. Delivery is casual, unrehearsed, mid-breath, sometimes trailing off.

CONTINUITY: The suite matches @image1 in both interior sequences. Hair, necklace, ring, face, body proportions, and outfit details remain identical throughout.

PHYSICS: Loose knit slides on the shoulder with every arm movement. Wavy hair lags a frame behind head turns. Bedding creases under her weight. Step energy is visible in every HELD frame.

LIGHTING: Shots 1–4 use cool daylight from the curtains as key and warm cove LED as fill. Shot 5 uses corridor light. Shots 6–7 use hard street daylight and warm diner practicals. Shot 8 uses lamps and cove light only.

AUDIO: Diegetic only, from the same camera — room tone, footsteps, door, traffic, sirens, steam vents, diner clatter, and wind. Ambience ducks under her lines. No music.

LOCKS: Photoreal live action, 4K detail, fine grain, warm consumer-camera color, mild rolling shutter and auto-exposure hunting. She is the only person who speaks. Background figures are anonymous and unfocused. No subtitles.

Prompt to video 

CINEMATIC FANTASY | THE BABY DRAGON

Format: 16:9 | Duration: 25 seconds | Photorealistic CGI

Scene & Atmosphere:

Create a breathtaking, cinematic fantasy short set inside a cozy medieval winter cabin. The interior features dark, rough stone walls, a rustic wooden floor, a small frosted window overlooking a snowy pine forest, and an empty stone fireplace. Cold blue winter light filters through the window, creating a beautiful contrast with the warm golden glow that gradually fills the room. Use shallow depth of field, subtle handheld camera movement, realistic textures, fine film grain, and an intimate, heartwarming atmosphere.

Main Characters:

The Woman: A young woman with long, wavy dark brown hair, wearing a black wool cloak over a dark, rustic dress. She shivers from the freezing temperature, with her breath visible in the cold air. Her expressions are gentle, natural, and full of warmth.

The Baby Dragon: An adorable, cat-sized baby dragon with pearly white and pale pink shimmering skin, enormous amber eyes, delicate frilly ears, translucent pink wings with intricate rose-colored veins, and a long, slender tail. Its movements are lifelike, innocent, playful, and emotionally expressive.

Scene 1 | 0–6 Seconds: A Magical Encounter

Begin with a cinematic wide shot of the freezing cabin. The woman sits beside the cold stone fireplace, hugging herself to keep warm. Her breath forms delicate clouds in the chilly air. A tiny baby dragon waddles across the wooden floor, its little tail trailing behind. It climbs beside the fireplace, and the woman gently strokes its head. The dragon looks up at her with curious, sparkling amber eyes.

Scene 2 | 6–12 Seconds: The Tiny Sneeze

Transition into an intimate close-up of the baby dragon's face. Its eyes slowly close, its tiny nostrils twitch, and it prepares to sneeze. A little puff of smoke escapes from its nose. The dragon opens its eyes in surprise, looking adorably confused and embarrassed. The woman smiles warmly, leans closer, and gently encourages it to try again. The dragon scrunches its face, preparing for another sneeze.

Scene 3 | 12–17 Seconds: A Spark of Magic

Capture a close two-shot as the baby dragon suddenly sneezes again. This time, a tiny burst of golden-orange flame shoots from its mouth and ignites the dry twigs inside the fireplace. The flames begin to dance, casting beautiful golden reflections across the stone walls. The woman bursts into joyful laughter, clasping her hands as the warm light illuminates her face. The baby dragon looks at the newly lit fire with pride and innocent amazement.

Scene 4 | 17–25 Seconds: Warmth and Affection

The cabin is now filled with a cozy, golden glow as the fire crackles gently. The woman carefully wraps the tiny dragon in a thick, soft sheepskin fur. The dragon climbs into her lap, curls up comfortably, and nuzzles against her cheek. End with an emotional cinematic close-up of the woman gently touching her forehead to the dragon's snout while stroking its tiny head. The dragon purrs softly as they share a tender moment beside the glowing fireplace.

Cinematic Style & Sound Design:

Ultra-realistic live-action aesthetic with photorealistic CGI, detailed dragon skin, beautifully translucent wings, believable creature animation, expressive eyes, natural human movements, cinematic composition, soft volumetric lighting, realistic fire simulation, and smooth transitions. Begin with icy blue tones and gradually transition into rich amber and golden hues as the fireplace comes alive.

Sound design includes howling winter wind outside, soft breathing, tiny dragon footsteps, a cute sneeze, a gentle burst of flame, crackling fire, and emotional piano accompanied by delicate orchestral strings during the final scene.

Negative Prompt:

No text, no watermark, no subtitles, no distorted faces, no extra limbs, no malformed wings, no unnatural movements, no flickering character designs, no inconsistent character appearance, no cartoon style, no plastic textures, no scary or aggressive dragon, no sudden scene changes, and no unrealistic lighting.

items.prompt:
PROMPT:

<inputs>

Defaults: product name LOUD ONE; 1920 × 1080; 30 fps; exactly 24 seconds and 720 frames; a cobalt-blue handheld music device with a large orange control, black LED display, speaker grille, silver hardware, and connected red and black cables.

Keep the reference's on-device copy unless replacement copy is supplied. Treat the preorder message as artwork for this recreation; do not invent a working purchase link.
</inputs>

<direction>
Create an energetic, glossy 3D product film with Higgsfield Katana and Claude Motion. The central idea is that a hummed idea travels through a playful world of musical hardware and becomes something ready to share.

The journey is HUM → SHAPE → DROP, ending with LOUD ONE.

Build a coherent floating installation in an open blue environment. The camera travels between physical objects suspended around a tall chrome mast: the hero device, speech-bubble display, horns, a recording light, meter, cassette, speaker stack, and LED letter panels.

The background is a saturated sky-blue to pale blue-gray gradient. Keep it spacious and luminous. There is no room, floor, horizon line, editor panel, or storyboard strip.

Use rounded industrial design, polished colored plastic, brushed and polished metal, dark rubber, and black perforated display surfaces. Objects should feel fabricated and dimensional even when their arrangement is playful.

Approximate palette: cobalt #173BD5, sky blue #158CEC, pale blue-gray #DCEAF1, orange #F34A13, cream #E8E5DE, violet #7137C4, lime #A9D53C, amber #E5AD35, and near-black #10151C. Refine against the reference.

Light the scene with large soft sources and sharp enough reflections to reveal the materials. Keep contact shadows between assembled parts. Preserve bright chrome highlights without losing detail in the white housing.

Use wide-angle product cinematography: close passes, changing perspective, orbiting, foreground occlusion, tilts, and fast travel between stations. Slow down when a message needs to be read.

Most typography belongs on physical objects. LED lettering should be made from a consistent dot grid. The main device types in white with an orange cursor; speech-bubble screens use warm-white dots, with orange emphasis; directional signs use amber.

Maintain the small HIGGSFIELD / CLAUDE MOTION badge at the upper-right as a separate overlay. Keep it fixed while the camera moves.

Avoid flat screenshots pretending to be 3D, unrelated montage inserts, excessive lens distortion, random glitch effects, or floating text detached from the objects.
</direction>

<structure>
Use these approximate reconstruction beats. Refine transitions against the reference while preserving the full 24-second runtime.

0:00–0:02.6 / HUM INTO THE DEVICE
Open close to the cobalt-blue hero device at an angle. Its rounded rectangular housing fills much of the image.

Show the recessed black LED display, speaker slots, small circular metal grille, top cable connections, LOUD ONE label, and large orange circular control surrounded by a ridged silver ring.

Type “hum me something...” across the display with an orange insertion cursor. Reveal the lettering as discrete LED states. As the camera approaches, change the screen to a recording treatment with a red REC indicator and an orange waveform.

Move across the front toward the orange control. Let changing reflections reveal the blue casing and machined ring. Keep the device stable as a rigid object.

0:02.6–0:05.6 / EVERY HIT STARTS AS A HUM
Pull away and travel toward a cream speech-bubble-shaped display mounted high on the chrome mast.

The housing has a soft rectangular screen and a pointed lower-left tail. A thin antenna extends upward; a black cable and red coiled cable connect below.

Begin with an empty black display, then reveal:
“EVERY HIT
STARTS AS A HUM.”

Use warm-white pixel lettering, centered inside the physical screen. Arrive at a readable angle and hold the finished sentence briefly.

Below the display, show a dark metal collar and several small colorful horn speakers. Keep the mechanical connections plausible.

0:05.6–0:08.2 / FOLLOW THE SOUND
Move down and around the mast. Pass the horn cluster, chrome brackets, exposed connectors, and coiled wires.

Reveal a glowing red “ON AIR” sign. Continue past a vertical meter containing circular lamps that rise through green, yellow, and red.

Use changes in distance and perspective to connect the objects. Let the hero device remain visible farther away on its cables.

Add a few suspended green and purple waveform-like squiggles, but keep them secondary. Use the mast, cables, and nearby objects to preserve spatial orientation through the fast camera travel.

0:08.2–0:10.6 / SHAPE IT
Travel toward a large floating cassette. Show it turning from an oblique view into a readable frontal presentation.

Build a dark blue-gray shell with a cream label, two visible reels, transparent windows, screws, seams, and an orange slider along the upper edge.

Main label:
“SHAPE IT.”

Small selectable style labels:
“LO-FI”
“HOUSE”
“FUNK”
“DISCO”

Move the orange control across the choices while the cassette shifts slightly in space. Give the reels subtle rotation. Preserve crisp readable text and realistic thickness at the casing edges.

Use a passing edge or fast turn to carry the camera into the next station.

0:10.6–0:13.5 / DROP IT
Find a narrow black LED sign above a floating audio stack.

Animate amber directional arrows into:
“DROP IT.”

Travel down the stack. Include a small black speaker, a purple rectangular unit, a yellow drum-like speaker body, a cream speaker with an orange cone, and a broad cobalt unit at the bottom.

Add a glossy red exclamation mark beneath the stack. Let the objects respond with controlled movement as the camera passes.

Keep speaker cones circular and their movement axial. Make this section feel like the energy of the musical idea has increased.

0:13.5–0:16.4 / SPELL OUT LOUD
Swing across a group of separate square black LED panels mounted along slender supports.

Reveal the letters L, O, U, D in amber dots. Individual panels rotate or pass through different orientations as the camera moves.

The letters should be legible at their key moments, with the full arrangement becoming understandable through the travel. Maintain the same world, lighting, and hardware language.

Use a fast but readable camera arc to return toward the speech-bubble display. Let a few rounded orange and purple shapes pass in the foreground.

0:16.4–0:20.4 / IDEAS, OUT LOUD
Return to the cream speech-bubble display.

Briefly show a small waveform, then reveal:
“IDEAS,
OUT LOUD.”

Keep IDEAS and OUT warm white. Make LOUD orange.

Hold a readable three-quarter view while the installation moves subtly. Keep the horn cluster, collar, hanging cables, green squiggle, and distant DROP IT sign visible as secondary details.

Near the end of this section, change the display to:
“LOUD
ONE”

Use a fast pullback to reconnect the display with the wider installation.

0:20.4–0:24 / PRODUCT HERO
Bring the cobalt device back into the foreground, suspended by its black and red cables.

Settle it left of center at a flattering three-quarter angle. The large orange control, chrome ring, speaker slots, and rounded casing must remain recognizable.

Place the four amber LED letter panels spelling LOUD to the right, arranged along their slender supports.

Change the device display from “LOUD ONE” to “PRE-ORDER NOW.”

End with a readable hero composition and subtle residual movement. Hold long enough to recognize the product and CTA. Do not force a loop or add an unrelated end card.
</structure>

<build>
1. Use an editable 3D scene and camera in the supported Katana/Claude Motion workflow. Three-dimensional objects must retain their shapes during camera travel. Use the available 3D renderer or supported scene pipeline rather than flattening the whole film into image cards.

2. Build a reusable asset library: hero device, orange dial, LED display surface, speech-bubble housing, mast, horns, ON AIR sign, meter, cassette and slider, speaker components, letter panels, cables, and decorative waveform shapes.

3. Keep geometry, materials, displayed text, lights, camera paths, animation, and branding individually editable. Centralize product name, messages, colors, and beat timings.

4. Place all stations in a shared scene. Plan the camera route before polishing detail. Use foreground objects and whip movements to bridge sections, keeping changes of direction physically understandable.

5. Use a master time function with 720 output frames at 30 fps. Seed randomness. Make each frame directly seekable and repeatable; avoid animation that depends on previous playback.

6. Construct cables with spline-based geometry. Keep endpoints attached to their ports. Give cable curves and suspended devices a small amount of secondary movement that settles after major camera or object actions.

7. Render LED text with proper display-space perspective and a stable dot grid. Use crisp message changes rather than morphing letters into unreadable intermediate glyphs.

8. Use motion blur for fast travel and passing objects, then restore clarity during text holds. Adjust focus for each subject rather than keeping the entire installation equally sharp.

9. Keep the top-right HIGGSFIELD / CLAUDE MOTION badge in screen space. It must not inherit scene blur, perspective, or exposure changes. Supply an unbranded export too if requested.

10. Inspect the supplied audio to place accents. If a new score is needed, propose a playful electronic groove that builds from a simple hummed motif into a fuller arrangement. This is a sound direction, not a claim about the source track.

11. Add focused sound details: a recording click, dial tick, relay or lamp activation, cassette movement, speaker pulse, and restrained pass-by sounds. Let the DROP IT moment receive a stronger musical accent. Keep the final product hold musically resolved.

12. Render a preview first. Check the whole camera route and every text hold before final-quality lighting and export.

Deliver KATANA_Pack_1_LOUD_ONE_1080p_30fps.mp4, the editable project or source, organized assets, and separate audio stems where available.

The hero product is LOUD ONE. Do not substitute PHYLLA or the OBSCURA branding from other references.

Keep the large orange dial on the same side of the device throughout. Maintain cable ports, screen placement, grille layout, and physical scale.

LED text lives inside the screens and signs. It must not slide independently of their surfaces.

Do not detach cable ends during the camera moves. Avoid cable intersections with the hero device and screen housing.

items.post_text:
I used Opus 5.5 to make a motion design video about Haiku

This is 100% motion graphics and code

Short story about Opus delegating small tasks to Haiku

Prompt in the comments https://t.co/hgBWx3DSEg https://t.co/KYAafB8sHp
items.prompt:
The full prompt below. It called a few tools to help get to the end result:
- @ChatGPT image for storyboarding
- @ElevenLabs for voice and music

Art style inspired by @jake11moran 

Total cost was under $10 and 3h

-------------
You're directing a 20-second animated short about the Claude Haiku 5.5 release. You're the director, the art department, the animator, the sound designer and the QA team, and you have real tools to call.

I'm giving you the idea, the tools and the quality bar. Everything else, from the beats to the look to the jokes, is yours to design. I trust your taste more than a beat sheet I could write. Your capabilities are far beyond what you assume, so work like it: plan carefully, push the craft, and use the tools and the time this deserves. Spend generously where it improves the film and economically everywhere else.

Final output: `out/level3.mp4`, 1920×1080, 30fps, exactly 20.0 seconds, with voices, music and sound design. At the end, you'll also save your process as a reusable skill.

---

## 1. The idea

**Opus is overloaded with work it shouldn't be doing.** It's buried in small, repetitive tasks: summaries, classifications, lookups, compactions. Then it has a realization: it can hand all of that to Haiku. It calls Haiku, Haiku arrives fast and clears the pile, and Opus is finally free to do the hard, important work it's built for.

That's the premise. How you tell it is up to you: the staging, gags, rhythm, camera, character beats, what the eureka moment looks like, how Haiku arrives, and how the delegation plays out. Sonnet can appear if it earns its place.

**Fixed points:**
- 20.0 seconds, 16:9.
- Opus and Haiku are characters in the same family as the Claude character.
- The film must read with the sound off.
- The ending respects reality: Haiku takes the volume, and Opus keeps the hard thinking. Anthropic says Opus 5.5 and Sonnet 5.5 remain the better choice for complex agentic coding, so Haiku is never shown replacing Opus.

---

## 2. Style reference

The reference is Jake Moran's "Animated agent session story": https://t.co/0mboS9hlPO. It was made with this skill: https://t.co/6LVaMXKNbe. Read the skill, including its references on motion and the room.

Take from it:
- The hand-drawn watercolour-on-paper look.
- A cozy room as a world.
- Cartoon blocks with faces as characters.
- Physical paper props that carry the story (paper planes as tasks).
- A score that's cued to every action.

Don't copy it. Use it as a starting point and push it further: richer staging, better acting from the characters, more cinematic camera, and a stronger hook. It should look like it belongs to the same family, made by someone who studied it closely.

---

## 3. Facts (lock these before any creative work)

Fetch https://t.co/XkHMkItEou and write `facts.json`: every claim you might use, each with the exact supporting sentence from the page. Only claims in `facts.json` may appear on screen or in dialogue.

This is a story first, so use one or two facts at most, woven into the world rather than presented as slides. For example, a price tag being re-stamped, or Haiku's speed shown rather than stated. The film must end on a card with **Claude Haiku 5.5**.

---

## 4. Audience and hook

The audience is AI and developer Twitter/X: people who use Claude every day and know the model names and the jokes about them. Before writing the treatment:
- **Research:** spend a little time on how people currently talk about Opus, Sonnet and Haiku, and what's being said about this launch. Find one or two references or running jokes this audience would recognize and enjoy. Use them only if they fit the story naturally. Never use real people or brand logos.
- **The hook:** the first second has to work as a still frame on a busy timeline. Someone scrolling should instantly see "a character drowning in work" and want to see what happens.
- **Text on screen:** this is motion design that tells a story, not a lyric video. Use text sparingly and only where it adds something: a beat the picture can't carry alone, the fact stamp, and the end card. Integrate it into the world (painted, stamped, written in marker) rather than overlaying it.

---

## 5. Tools

The keys are in `.env`. Pick the best tool for each job, and tell me which you chose and why.

| Tool | Key | Use it for |
|---|---|---|
| Web search and fetch | — | Source page, style reference, audience research |
| Higgsfield (connector) | — | Image generation; call `models_explore` first to pick the best model for flat illustrated characters. Also music or sound effects if its audio models are the best fit. |
| GPT Image (OpenAI) | `OPENAI_API_KEY` | A second image model. Test both on the same prompt and keep whichever matches the style better. |
| ElevenLabs | `ELEVENLABS_API_KEY` | Character voices, sound effects, and music (Eleven Music) |
| Remotion | — | The film itself |
| ffmpeg + Python | — | Audio analysis, frame extraction, checks |
| Subagents | — | Parallel research and independent review |

---

## 6. Order of work

### Step 1: Treatment
Write `treatment.md`:
- Your take on the story in one paragraph.
- The beat sheet with timings.
- What happens in each shot: camera, acting, the gag.
- Where the music hits.
- What each character says.
- Which fact appears and how.
- Why this version is the strongest way to tell it.

Write two or three distinct treatments, then pick one and explain why.

### Step 2: Style bible
Write `style/bible.md`:
- Palette: 6 colours maximum, with hex values and a reason for each.
- Ink line rules: weight, and the "boiling" redraw jitter.
- Watercolour and paper texture.
- Lighting.
- Type: local font files only.
- Character design rules for Opus and Haiku: size ratio, shapes, how each one moves, and their expression set.

### Step 3: Key art (images as the base, no video generation)
The generated images are your key frames and design references. You are the in-betweener. Generate:
1. **Style frames:** 3 options of the world. Pick one.
2. **Character sheets:** Opus and Haiku, each with front, three-quarter and side views and their full expression set. Use the chosen style frame as a reference so everything shares one world.
3. **Key poses:** one image per key pose in your treatment (roughly 6–10), each built from the character sheets and the style frame, matching the camera and composition of the shot.

Put everything on one contact sheet.

**Stop and wait for my approval** before building anything.

The images are references. The final film is drawn in code to match them, and generated images never appear on screen. Trace the shapes, poses, proportions and composition from the key art into SVG, and animate between them.

### Step 4: Audio first
The film's timing comes from the audio.
1. **Voices:** audition at least 2 ElevenLabs voices per character. Opus should feel warm, low and deliberate. Haiku should feel quick, bright and eager. Generate each line separately, with 2 takes, and keep the best delivery.
2. **Music:** generate a track that fits your treatment, about 22s long, with its structure matching your beats: for example, a drop when Haiku arrives. If the generated track won't land on your beats, trim and offset it with ffmpeg rather than changing the picture.
3. **Sound effects:** a sound for every physical action. Paper, whooshes, impacts, the lightbulb, stamps.
4. **Timing map:** detect the music's beat onsets and write `timing.json`. It holds every beat time, the drop frame, each voice line's start and end frames, and every key action snapped to the nearest beat. All animation timing reads from `timing.json`, with nothing hardcoded.
5. Play me the audio-only mix before building the picture.

### Step 5: Build in Remotion
- **Components:** one per character, prop and set piece. Story beats live as data in `story.json`.
- **Drawing:** watercolour fills via SVG turbulence and displacement filters, a multiply-blended paper texture, and boiling ink lines.
- **Motion craft:** anticipation before every big action, follow-through after, squash and stretch, springs for landings, arcs for every moving object, and no linear easing.
- **Acting:** the characters have to perform. Give them readable poses, holds where the audience needs to read a face, and timing that's funny.
- **Mouths:** mouth shapes driven by the voice track's loudness. They must be still when the character is silent.
- **Camera:** push-ins, a whip or a shake where it helps. Motivate every camera move.
- **Mix:** music, voices and sound effects on separate layers. Duck the music under dialogue.

---

## 7. Verification loops (do not skip any)

1. **Key-pose match:** at every key pose, render the frame and compare it side by side with its key art. Write what differs and fix it.
2. **Sound-off read:** render a silent cut. A fresh subagent that has seen nothing else reviews a contact sheet at 2 frames per second and retells the story. If it can't, the staging failed. Fix it and repeat.
3. **Sync check:** list every catch, landing, stamp and dialogue line with its actual frame vs its `timing.json` target. Everything must be within 1 frame.
4. **Fact check:** every word on screen and in dialogue, matched to `facts.json`. Cut anything unmatched.
5. **Technical:** duration exactly 20.0s, stereo audio, peaks below −1 dBFS, no unintended dead air.
6. **Director's review:**
   - Watch the whole film at least twice as frames.
   - Write a brutal critique as the most demanding motion designer you know: what feels assembled, what's slow, what doesn't land.
   - Fix the top 3 issues, then review again.
   - Only then hand it over, with a 10-frame contact sheet.

---

## 8. Package it as a skill

Save the full pipeline as `.claude/skills/launch-film/SKILL.md`, so that next time *"Make a launch film for [URL] about [idea]"* is enough.

The skill should include:
- The fact lock
- The treatment process
- The style bible as a reference file
- The key-art process with both image models
- Voice auditions
- Music and sound effects
- The timing map
- The reusable Remotion components
- Every verification loop

---

## Approval gates
1. `facts.json` and the chosen treatment
2. Style bible, character sheets and key poses → **wait for my approval**
3. Audio-only mix and `timing.json`
4. Final film, contact sheet and critique
5. Skill

Keep a task list throughout. At each gate, show me the work, not a description of it.

items.post_text:
Image: Midjourney (Scene) + ChatGPT (Characters)
Video : Seedance 2.0

15s ultra-cinematic wuxia sword duel

[0:00–0:01] HIGH-SPEED COLLISION
Extreme low-angle 24mm ground-skimming tracking shot, centimeters above ancient stone pavement. Burgundy warrior and white-robed swordswoman charge head-on at full sprint, neither decelerating. At the crossing point: CLANG—CLANG—CLANG, three exchanges inside one second, blades reduced to fragmented silver arcs and glints. Camera threads the gap between them.

[0:01–0:03] CROSSING ATTACK → INSTANT PIVOT
Fast lateral tracking. Both pivot the moment they pass. He: reverse horizontal slash mid-turn. She: ducks under, simultaneous thrust to the ribs. He: downward blade rotation, deflects. She: converts the failed thrust into a rising diagonal cut. He: intercepts. 5–7 contacts in ~2s, zero pauses, overlapping silver trails.

[0:03–0:05] SPIRAL CLOSE-QUARTERS EXCHANGE
35mm medium close-up, rapid orbital arc. Extreme close measure.
He: horizontal slash → reverse slash → descending diagonal → immediate thrust.
She: parry → body rotation → deflection → low counter-slash → rising interception.
One unbroken flow. Blades vanish into blur and reappear only at contact. Sparks strictly on true blade impact. Robes wrap and twist under centrifugal force.

[0:05–0:07] AERIAL PURSUIT
She leaps backward onto the next flight of the monumental staircase; he pursues instantly. Camera cranes up alongside. She strikes airborne, he blocks while ascending; multiple mid-air contacts. She completes one full aerial rotation into a descending diagonal strike; he intercepts and redirects it laterally. Near-simultaneous landing, attacking again before their footing settles.

[0:07–0:09] ULTRA-FAST STAIRCASE DUEL
Low-angle leading shot, pulling back rapidly up the stairs. Both sprint upward while fighting, never breaking stride. He attacks from alternating angles; she blocks in backward ascent. Near-invisible blades, streaks crossing frame: left → right → diagonal → vertical → thrust → deflection. 8–12 distinct sword actions in 2s, compressed into a barely readable storm of steel. Operator slightly behind the action: controlled vérité urgency.

[0:09–0:11] WHIP-PAN BLADE STORM
85mm telephoto compression, extreme close combat. Rapid whip-pans between inserts: hands on hilts, boots shifting footwork, twisting robes, eyes reading the opponent's shoulders, blades colliding. The lens cannot fully resolve every movement; several attacks land partly off-frame, so the duel outpaces the cinematography itself. Sword speed at near-visual limit. No supernatural energy waves, no large magical VFX: only steel, sparks, wind, fabric, kinetic force.

[0:11–0:13] AGGRESSIVE COUNTERATTACK
He abruptly escalates into a relentless chain: horizontal slash, diagonal slash, reverse cut, thrust, low sweep, immediate overhead strike. She blocks everything while retreating fast down several steps. Frontal pull-back tracking on her; her expression stays intensely focused. He wears a subtle sinister smile mid-assault. Burgundy sleeves and long black hair whip through frame. Blades nearly indistinguishable; impacts become rapid rhythm: CLANG—CLANG—CLANG—CLANG

[0:13–0:15] CONTINUOUS BLADE STOR
No climax explosion, no finishing move, no victory pose, no separation, no cut to black. The tempo climbs further.
Extreme dynamic 35mm parallel tracking at high speed. She breaks rhythm and drives forward in a fierce counterattack; he gives ground, parrying. Roles reversed, they race laterally across the vast Tibetan stone terrace in nonstop exchange. Swords almost fully unreadable: dozens of fragmented streaks, brief glints, sparks. Feet never stop, bodies rotate, robes stream in Himalayan wind. Palace columns rush past as background parallax; the cloud ocean churns below the cliff. Final 0.5s: he throws a rapid diagonal attack; she intercepts and rotates straight into another counter.
HARD CUT ON ACTION: both still in motion, swords mid-exchange.

Tiny warrior, giant dragon, and an unexpected friendship.

Created with MiniMax H3 Fast

Prompt:

A cinematic, ultra-realistic fantasy scene featuring an adorable fluffy ginger-and-white kitten warrior wearing miniature silver medieval armor, a flowing cream-colored cape, and carrying a tiny sword, standing bravely in a misty green meadow facing a massive, fearsome dragon covered in dark, rugged scales, sharp horns, and powerful leathery wings. The camera captures dramatic low-angle shots, close-ups of the kitten gripping its sword, and intense shots of the dragon lowering its enormous head toward the tiny warrior. The kitten initially stands courageously, but as the dragon approaches, it becomes frightened and drops its sword, looking up with teary eyes and a trembling expression. She is always relaxed and gently smiling, never rushed, never out of breath.

**0–5s:** Teacher steps out of a classroom door, one hand holding the book, the other casually pushing a charging zombie student aside as he stumbles past. Cut to a close-up profile of her calm smile, glasses catching the light, classroom blurred behind. She raises one finger to her ear with a playful, relaxed gesture while students lie collapsed behind her.

**5–12s:** Wide shot down the long corridor. A horde of dark-clad zombie students runs toward her while a few already crawl on the floor. She stands still, hugging the book at her side. One zombie lunges; she sidesteps and redirects him with a light palm push so he spins away. Another leans against the wall, dazed.

**12–20s:** Low-angle shot of her stiletto heels: she kicks one zombie into a handstand-style flip, his body toppling in slow motion. Close-up of a zombie screaming, then her open palm gently stopping his face in the frame. Quick, elegant counters: wrist twist, hip toss, heel tap, all effortless.

**20–25s:** Wide top-down corridor shot. The whole horde now lies sprawled across the floor in heaps, groaning. She walks back through the door, straightens her blouse, picks up her book from the desk and turns to the class with a warm smile. Subtitle-style line in her mouth: "Now, where were we?"

**25–30s:** Classroom interior. Students in navy blazers sit at wooden desks, stunned and wide-eyed, a girl with a short black bob in front staring at the teacher. Close-up profile of the teacher in front of the green chalkboard, glasses reflecting window light, giving a calm, gentle, slightly mischievous smile. Slow push-in on her face to end.

**Style notes:** Comedic contrast: calm, graceful teacher vs chaotic zombie horde. Fight moves are clean and light, no heavy contact. Subtle slow-motion on flips and kicks, then snap back to real speed. Sound: running footsteps, heel clicks, soft whooshes, a playful light jazz groove, quiet classroom ambience at the end.
